questions.question: What is a user in Linux?
questions.answer: A Linux user is an account that allows a person or a process to log into the system and use system resources such as files, commands, processes, and devices. Users are identified internally by the kernel using a unique numeric UID.

questions.question: What are the three types of Linux users?
questions.answer: 1. Root User (UID 0) — superuser with full administrative privileges. 2. Normal User (UID 1000+) — created by admin for human use, limited privileges. 3. System User (UID 1–999) — created for background services and daemons, no interactive login.

questions.question: What is the difference between /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow?
questions.answer: /etc/passwd stores general user information (username, UID, GID, home directory, shell) and is world-readable — anyone can view it. /etc/shadow stores the actual encrypted (hashed) passwords and is readable only by root, preventing normal users from even seeing the password hashes.

questions.question: What does the UID of a Linux user represent?
questions.answer: UID (User ID) is a unique numeric identifier assigned to every user account. The Linux kernel uses UIDs internally to determine file ownership and access control. Root always has UID 0. Normal users typically start at UID 1000. System users are in the range 1–999.

questions.question: What is the purpose of sudo?
questions.answer: sudo (superuser do) allows an authorised normal user to execute a specific command with root-level privileges temporarily, without switching to the root account. It is controlled by the /etc/sudoers file, which lists which users and groups can use sudo and which commands they can run.

questions.question: Explain what r, w, and x mean in Linux file permissions.
questions.answer: r (read=4): For files — can view content. For directories — can list contents with ls. w (write=2): For files — can modify the file. For directories — can create or delete files inside. x (execute=1): For files — can run it as a program. For directories — can cd into it and access its contents.

questions.question: What does chmod 644 mean?
questions.answer: chmod 644 sets permissions to rw-r--r--. The first digit 6 (4+2=rw-) gives the owner read and write. The second digit 4 (4+0+0=r--) gives the group read only. The third digit 4 gives others read only. This is the standard permission for regular files.

questions.question: What is a Linux group and why is it useful?
questions.answer: A group is a collection of user accounts that share the same access permissions to files and directories. Instead of granting permissions to individual users, an admin assigns permissions to a group and adds users to it. This makes managing access for teams much more efficient.

questions.question: What is the primary group of a user?
questions.answer: When a user account is created in Linux, a group with the same name as the username is automatically created — this is the primary group. Every file created by that user will belong to their primary group by default.

questions.question: What does chown do and when would you use it?
questions.answer: chown (change owner) changes the user and/or group ownership of a file or directory. You use it when a file needs to be owned by a different user — for example, after uploading web files as root, you run chown -R www-data:www-data /var/www/html so the web server process (running as www-data) can read the files.

questions.question: Describe a situation where you needed to troubleshoot a permission denied error on a Linux server.
questions.answer: (Situation) A web application was returning 403 Forbidden errors after deployment to EC2. (Task) I needed to identify and fix the permission issue without disrupting the service. (Action) I ran 'ls -la /var/www/html' and saw the files were owned by root:root with 640 permissions. The Apache process ran as www-data, which fell in the 'others' category — others had no read permission. I ran 'sudo chown -R www-data:www-data /var/www/html' to fix ownership. (Result) The web application became accessible immediately without any code changes.

questions.question: You added a user to a group but 'groups username' doesn't show the new group. What could be the issue?
questions.answer: (Situation) After running usermod -aG developers alice, the groups command still did not show the developers group. (Task) Identify why the group change is not reflected. (Action) I asked alice to log out completely and log back in. The issue is that group membership changes do not apply to active sessions — the kernel only reads group memberships at login time. (Result) After re-logging in, 'groups alice' showed developers in the list.

questions.question: A new developer joins your team and needs sudo access on an EC2 Amazon Linux instance. Walk me through the process.
questions.answer: (Situation) New developer Bob needs sudo access on our Amazon Linux EC2 instance. (Task) Grant sudo access securely without sharing root credentials. (Action) 1. SSH as ec2-user. 2. Create Bob's account: sudo useradd -m -s /bin/bash bob. 3. Set a password: sudo passwd bob. 4. Add bob to the wheel group: sudo usermod -aG wheel bob. 5. Verify: sudo su - bob, then run 'sudo whoami' — should return 'root'. (Result) Bob has sudo access. His name is not added to /etc/sudoers directly — he inherits access through the wheel group, keeping sudoers clean.

questions.question: Your script fails to execute with 'Permission denied'. How do you diagnose and fix it?
questions.answer: (Situation) Running './deploy.sh' returned Permission denied. (Task) Make the script executable without compromising security. (Action) Ran 'ls -l deploy.sh' — output showed -rw-r--r-- (644). The owner execute bit was missing. Ran 'chmod u+x deploy.sh' (or chmod 755 if others also need to run it). Verified with 'ls -l' — showed -rwxr--r-- or -rwxr-xr-x. (Result) Script executed successfully.

questions.question: How do you create a shared team directory where all team members can collaborate and no one outside can access it?
questions.answer: (Situation) A team of 3 developers needs a shared project directory on a Linux server. (Task) Create a secure collaboration space. (Action) 1. groupadd devteam. 2. usermod -aG devteam alice; usermod -aG devteam bob; usermod -aG devteam carol. 3. mkdir /shared/project. 4. chown root:devteam /shared/project. 5. chmod 2770 /shared/project (SGID + rwx for owner and group, nothing for others). (Result) All three can read, write, and create files. New files automatically belong to devteam. Outsiders cannot even list the directory.

questions.question: You find a file with chmod 777 on a production server. What do you do?
questions.answer: (Situation) Security audit found /var/www/html/config.php with permissions 777. (Task) Fix without breaking the application. (Action) First identified who runs the web server: ps aux | grep apache showed www-data. Checked current owner: ls -l config.php showed root:root. Changed to: chown www-data:www-data config.php && chmod 640 config.php — owner (www-data) gets rw, group (www-data) gets r, others get nothing. Tested the application. (Result) Application still worked, file is no longer world-readable or world-writable.

questions.question: A junior admin accidentally ran 'usermod -G wheel alice' instead of 'usermod -aG wheel alice'. What happened and how do you fix it?
questions.answer: (Situation) Without the -a flag, usermod -G replaces all secondary group memberships. Alice lost membership in all her other groups (developers, docker, etc.) and only belongs to wheel. (Task) Restore her group memberships. (Action) Check /etc/group to find which groups she should be in. Re-add her to each: sudo usermod -aG developers alice; sudo usermod -aG docker alice. Ask Alice to re-login to apply changes. (Result) This is why -aG is the safe and always-recommended flag for adding to groups.

questions.question: Explain the security principle behind why /etc/shadow was created separately from /etc/passwd.
questions.answer: (Situation) Originally, Linux stored password hashes in /etc/passwd, which was world-readable (any user could read it). (Task) Eliminate the security risk of exposing password hashes to all users. (Action) /etc/shadow was created to separate sensitive password data from general user information. /etc/passwd remains world-readable (many programs need it) but now only stores 'x' as a password placeholder. /etc/shadow stores the actual hashes and is readable only by root. (Result) Even if a normal user reads /etc/passwd, they cannot access hashes to attempt offline cracking.

questions.question: How would you audit who has sudo access on a Linux system?
questions.answer: (Situation) A security audit requires identifying all users with sudo privileges on an EC2 instance. (Task) Produce a complete list. (Action) 1. Check /etc/sudoers: sudo cat /etc/sudoers (look for user lines and %group lines). 2. Check /etc/sudoers.d/: sudo ls /etc/sudoers.d/ and read each file. 3. Check wheel/sudo group membership: grep 'wheel' /etc/group or getent group wheel. 4. Cross-reference with /etc/passwd to confirm accounts are active. (Result) A complete picture of who can escalate privileges on the system.

questions.question: A developer needs to run only the 'systemctl restart nginx' command as root — nothing else. How do you set this up?
questions.answer: (Situation) Developer Alice needs to restart nginx without full sudo access. (Task) Apply least privilege — only the specific command, no more. (Action) Run sudo visudo and add: alice ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/systemctl restart nginx. This allows alice to run that exact command with sudo but nothing else. (Result) Alice can run 'sudo systemctl restart nginx' successfully, but any other sudo command is denied. This follows the principle of least privilege.

questions.question: Design the permission scheme for a multi-tenant web hosting server where each customer has their own site directory and cannot access other customers' files.
questions.answer: Architecture: Create one group per customer (customer1, customer2). Create one system user per customer that the web server uses (web_cust1, web_cust2). Directory structure: /var/www/customer1 owned by web_cust1:customer1 with permissions 750 (rwxr-x---). The web server runs as each customer's system user via virtual host configuration. Each customer's login user is in their customer group but not others. Result: Customer1 can read/write their own directory, the web server can read it, and customer2 cannot list or access it at all.

questions.question: Explain how SUID, SGID, and Sticky Bit each solve a different real-world access control problem.
questions.answer: SUID solves: Allowing normal users to perform privileged actions on specific programs. Example: /usr/bin/passwd must write to /etc/shadow (root-only). SUID makes passwd run as root regardless of who calls it. SGID solves: Automatic group inheritance in collaborative directories. When a team shares /project with SGID, all files created there automatically belong to the project group — no manual chown needed. Sticky Bit solves: Protecting individual files in world-writable directories. In /tmp (chmod 1777), everyone can create files but cannot delete others' files. Without sticky bit, any user could delete any file in /tmp.

questions.question: A compromised normal user account is found on an EC2 instance. Walk through your incident response steps involving user and permission management.
questions.answer: Immediate: 1. Lock the account: sudo usermod -L compromised_user (prevents login, doesn't delete evidence). 2. Kill active sessions: sudo pkill -u compromised_user. Investigation: 3. Check /var/log/auth.log for sudo usage: grep compromised_user /var/log/auth.log. 4. Check what groups they were in: getent group | grep compromised_user. 5. Find files they own: find / -user compromised_user -ls. Remediation: 6. Rotate any secrets they had access to. 7. Review sudoers for overly broad permissions. 8. Remove from sudo/wheel if applicable: usermod -G '' compromised_user. Recovery: 9. Document findings. 10. Delete account when investigation is complete: userdel -r compromised_user.

questions.question: How does the Linux permission model implement the principle of least privilege, and how would you apply it to an EC2 instance setup?
questions.answer: The permission model implements least privilege through three layers: 1. User isolation — processes run as specific users (www-data, mysql) with only necessary access. 2. Group membership — users access shared resources only through explicit group additions. 3. Permission bits — files expose only necessary permissions (640 instead of 644 or 777). Applied to EC2: Create separate service accounts for each application. Web server reads /var/www (r--) but never writes production config. Database user owns /var/lib/mysql only. Application user in group 'app' for shared configs. No shared password — use SSH keys. Only one named admin in sudoers with logging enabled. This limits blast radius if any single component is compromised.

questions.question: Explain the security implications of the SUID bit on system binaries and how attackers abuse it.
questions.answer: SUID allows any user to execute a binary with its owner's (usually root's) privileges. Legitimate use: /usr/bin/passwd needs root to write /etc/shadow. Security risk: If a SUID binary has a vulnerability (buffer overflow, command injection), an attacker can exploit it to gain root access — even from a normal user account. Common attack pattern: Find SUID binaries with 'find / -perm -4000 -ls'. Identify vulnerable or misconfigured ones. Exploit to get a root shell. Hardening: Audit all SUID binaries regularly (find / -perm /4000). Remove SUID from any binary that does not strictly need it. Use nosuid mount options on filesystems where SUID binaries should not exist (e.g., /home, /tmp). This is a key concept in Linux privilege escalation — understanding it is essential for both security and DevOps roles.
